items.title: Kosher rules separate meat and dairy
items.claim: What are the main categories of kosher (kashrut) restrictions?

options.text: Permitted animals (mammals that chew cud and have cloven hooves; fish with fins and scales); ritual slaughter (shechita); separation of meat and dairy in cooking, eating and utensils; specific prohibitions including pork, shellfish, mixing milk and meat
Only meals at synagogue must be kosher

items.reveal:
The meat-dairy separation derives from three repetitions of 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). Rabbinic interpretation extended this to all mixing of meat and dairy.

Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 list permitted and forbidden animals. Pork and shellfish are the most widely known prohibitions; rabbit, camel and birds of prey are also forbidden.

Shechita is ritual slaughter by a trained shochet with a perfectly sharp knife in a single cut — designed to be quick and to drain blood. Some European countries (Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Belgian regions) have banned shechita without prior stunning on animal welfare grounds.
items.why: Religious practice is often embodied — daily eating, household kitchens, separate dishes. Kashrut is one of the clearest cases of belief expressed through bodily and domestic practice.

items.title: Muslims believe the Quran is the direct, unchanged word of God
items.claim: How do Muslims understand the origin of the Quran?

options.text: A collection of Muhammad's wise sayings, gathered over centuries
Revealed directly by God to Muhammad through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) over 23 years (610-632 CE), to be recited and transmitted unchanged in Arabic
A revised version of the Bible adapted for Arabia
A book written by Muhammad based on his teachings

items.reveal:
The word 'Quran' comes from the Arabic root q-r-' meaning 'to recite'. The first revelation (Sura 96, 'Iqra' — Recite!) at Mount Hira around 610 CE.

The Quran was compiled in written form under Caliph Uthman (around 650 CE), with non-conforming versions destroyed to ensure a single authoritative text. Muslims regard the Arabic text — not translations — as the Quran proper.

The Hadith (sayings of Muhammad) is a distinct category, recorded by his companions, with major Sunni collections by Bukhari (d. 870) and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 875).
items.why: The Quran's status differs sharply from how Christians treat the Bible (composed by human authors under divine inspiration). Islamic theology treats every Arabic word as direct divine speech — which is why translation is always a 'meaning of' the Quran.

items.title: Hindu deities are often understood as manifestations of one Brahman
items.claim: How does Hindu theology relate the many gods to Brahman?

options.text: Each god is wholly separate and independent

Many Hindus understand the gods as manifestations (devas) of one ultimate reality (Brahman) — though the relationship varies between traditions; the Rig Veda (1.164.46) says 'Truth is one; sages call it by many names'
There is only one god — Brahma alone

items.reveal:
The Trimurti (Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer) is one classical mapping of cosmic functions.

Vaishnavism centres on Vishnu and his avatars (Rama, Krishna). Shaivism centres on Shiva. Shaktism centres on Devi/Shakti (the divine feminine — Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati). Each tradition may treat its chosen deity as supreme.

The term 'henotheism' (worshipping one god while acknowledging others) was coined by Max Müller in the 19th century specifically to describe Vedic religion.
items.why: Calling Hinduism polytheistic or monotheistic both miss the structure. The 'many manifestations of one' framework is philosophically distinct — and shapes how Hindus actually relate to images and shrines.
